name: Russia-Ukraine war
summary: Russia invaded Ukraine on 24 February 2022, eight years after seizing Crimea and backing separatist forces in the Donbas. The drive on Kyiv failed within weeks, and the war became a grinding contest along a front running through the east and south, with both sides striking deep into the other's territory. Russia holds roughly a fifth of Ukraine and the fighting continues. ---

locations.name: Kyiv
locations.summary: Kyiv was Russia's first objective of the invasion. Troops advancing from Belarus reached the northern suburbs in February 2022 but failed to take the city and withdrew on 2 April, leaving mass killings of civilians behind them in Bucha and Irpin. The capital has faced no ground threat since, but is struck regularly by missiles and drones.

keyEvents.text: Russian troops crossed from Belarus and an airborne assault seized Hostomel airport north-west of the city.
Missiles struck the main television tower, killing five, and hit the ground beside the Babyn Yar Holocaust memorial.
An Iskander missile destroyed part of the Retroville shopping mall in Podilskyi district, killing at least eight.
Russian forces completed their withdrawal from Kyiv oblast, leaving mass killings of civilians documented at Bucha and Irpin.
keyEvents.note: CONTESTED: 2 April is when the withdrawal was declared complete and the Bucha killings became known; the Kyiv offensive is dated to 8 April in some accounts

keyEvents.text: Russia began mass missile strikes on Ukrainian cities two days after the Kerch bridge attack, hitting central Kyiv in the morning rush hour.
Shahed drones killed four people in a residential block in Shevchenkivskyi district, among them a woman six months pregnant.
More than fifty cruise missiles hit power infrastructure around the city, cutting water to about 80 per cent of the capital.
A strike on energy infrastructure cut running water across the whole city and killed a seventeen-year-old girl.
Russia fired around seventy-six missiles nationwide, more than half at Kyiv, in the largest attack on the capital to that date.
Russia's largest drone attack of the war to that date sent at least forty Shaheds over the city across more than five hours.
A drone attack surpassing the May record damaged a children's nursery and around two hundred buildings, wounding five.
A mass missile and drone assault killed thirty-three people in Kyiv, the deadliest attack on the capital's civilians of the war, and damaged the Lukianivska metro station being used as a shelter.
Russia used more Kinzhal missiles in one attack than at any point in the war, killing four people in Kyiv and wounding about seventy.
Missiles and drones destroyed the Trypilska thermal power plant, the largest generator supplying the capital and its region.
A cruise missile struck the Okhmatdyt children's hospital, killing two adults and injuring sixteen; the day's attack on the city killed thirty-three people in all.
A nationwide barrage struck the dam of the Kyiv hydroelectric plant and cut water on the right bank, though officials later said the dam held.
Missiles including a North Korean KN-23 killed thirteen people and injured more than ninety, the deadliest attack on the capital since 2022.
A mass drone and missile barrage killed twenty-eight people, twenty-three of them in a single nine-storey building, and wounded more than a hundred and thirty.
A barrage six days later killed nine people in Shevchenkivskyi district and damaged a school.
A direct hit on an apartment block in Sviatoshynskyi district killed thirty-one people, five of them children, and wounded a hundred and fifty-nine.
A combined drone and missile assault on central Kyiv killed twenty-three people and damaged the European Union delegation building and the British Council office.
keyEvents.note: CONTESTED toll: reported as at least 21 on the day, rising to 23 as bodies were recovered

keyEvents.text: In the largest air attack of the war to that date, 810 drones and 13 missiles, Russia struck the Cabinet of Ministers building for the first time.
One of the largest ballistic attacks on Ukraine's energy system since 2022 left the capital under more than twelve hours of emergency power cuts.
An overnight attack killed seven people and damaged a hospital, a school, the Azerbaijani embassy and sections of the district heating network.
keyEvents.note: CONTESTED date: the attack ran overnight and is dated to 13 November by some sources and 14 November by others

keyEvents.text: Russia fired an Oreshnik missile at the capital for only the second time in the war, killing four people, damaging the Qatari embassy and leaving nearly six thousand apartment buildings without heat.
Strikes on the energy system cut heating, power and water to roughly half the capital's apartment buildings in temperatures below minus ten.
The largest aerial attack of the war, 1,567 drones and 56 missiles, fell hardest on Kyiv and killed twenty-four people in the city after a residential block collapsed in Darnytskyi district.
A drone and missile assault struck more than thirty locations across every district of the city, killing at least twenty-five people.
A missile and drone attack killed fifteen people in the city and struck a school and a children's hospital in Solomianskyi district.
A drone struck the headquarters of the Security Service in central Kyiv, near the UNESCO-listed Saint Sophia Cathedral, wounding twelve.

locations.name: Kharkiv
locations.summary: Kharkiv is Ukraine's second city and sits thirty kilometres from the Russian border. Russian troops reached its outskirts in February 2022 and shelled it for months before Ukraine's September counteroffensive drove them out of the oblast; a second Russian push north of the city opened in May 2024 and stalled at Vovchansk. Its proximity to the border leaves it under near-daily glide bomb and drone attack.

keyEvents.text: Russian forces reached the city's outskirts and sustained shelling of residential districts began.
Two missiles struck the regional administration building on Freedom Square, killing 29.
keyEvents.note: CONTESTED toll: same-day reports said 6–10; 29 is the April 2022 confirmed figure

keyEvents.text: Ukraine's counteroffensive broke the front; Izium was retaken on 10 September and Russian forces were driven from most of the oblast.
Russia opened a second offensive into northern Kharkiv oblast, which stalled at Vovchansk.
A glide bomb hit the Epicentr hardware store, killing 19 and wounding more than 50.

locations.name: Pokrovsk
locations.summary: Pokrovsk was the road and rail hub supplying Ukrainian positions across the Donetsk front. Russian forces began pushing towards it in mid-2024, ground through the approaches for over a year, and claimed the city on 2 December 2025. Russian momentum stalled after its capture, and fighting has continued in the sectors east and north of the town.

keyEvents.text: Two Iskander missiles hit a hotel and an apartment block forty minutes apart, the second killing rescuers who had arrived after the first; 10 died and 82 were wounded.
Ukraine ordered the mandatory evacuation of families with children as Russian forces closed on the town.
Russia claimed the capture of the city after more than a year of fighting on its approaches.

locations.name: Donetsk
locations.summary: Donetsk was seized by Russian-backed forces in April 2014 and became the capital of the self-declared Donetsk People's Republic, which Russia annexed in September 2022. The city has been under Russian control for over a decade and now sits well behind the front line rather than on it. It is hit by Ukrainian shelling and drone strikes aimed at the military infrastructure inside it.

keyEvents.text: Separatists occupying the regional administration building declared the Donetsk People's Republic.
Fighting for Donetsk airport began; the terminal held out until separatist forces took it on 21 January 2015.
Russia signed treaties annexing Donetsk oblast along with Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson.

locations.name: Mariupol
locations.summary: Mariupol was besieged from the opening days of the invasion and destroyed in the taking. Russian aircraft bombed the drama theatre sheltering civilians on 16 March 2022, and the last defenders surrendered at the Azovstal steelworks on 20 May; estimates of the civilian dead run into the thousands. The city has been occupied since, and its port is now a Ukrainian drone target.

keyEvents.text: The city was fully encircled, cutting water, power and heat.
Russian aircraft bombed maternity hospital No. 3.
The drama theatre, sheltering civilians with "CHILDREN" written outside it, was bombed.
keyEvents.note: CONTESTED toll: Amnesty says at least 12 and likely many more; an AP investigation estimated around 600

keyEvents.text: The last defenders at the Azovstal steelworks surrendered and Russia declared full control.

locations.name: Zaporizhzhia
locations.summary: Zaporizhzhia city has never been taken, but the front line has sat some forty kilometres to its south since 2022, and Europe's largest nuclear plant — held by Russian forces at Enerhodar downriver since March 2022 — lies inside the same oblast. Ukraine's 2023 counteroffensive on this axis gained little ground. The city is struck regularly, including in a wave of attacks across Ukraine on 11 August 2026.

keyEvents.text: Russian forces seized the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant at Enerhodar, the first time an operating nuclear station had been taken in war.
Sixteen missiles hit a civilian convoy on the city's outskirts, killing 32, hours before Russia's annexation ceremony.
keyEvents.note: CONTESTED toll: same-day reports 23–30; 32 is the confirmed figure

keyEvents.text: Ukraine's southern counteroffensive opened on this axis and gained little ground over the summer.
keyEvents.note: CONTESTED date: ISW dates the onset to 4 June; most Western outlets reported the visible Zaporizhzhia push from 8 June

locations.name: Kherson
locations.summary: Kherson was the only regional capital Russia captured intact, falling on 2 March 2022 and held for eight months before Russian forces withdrew across the Dnipro on 11 November. The river now forms the front line and the city sits directly on it. It is shelled daily from the occupied left bank and has become known for drone attacks flown deliberately at civilians in the streets.

keyEvents.text: Kherson fell, the only Ukrainian regional capital captured in the invasion.
Russia annexed the oblast.
Ukrainian forces entered the city as Russian troops withdrew across the Dnipro.
The Kakhovka dam was breached, flooding the lower Dnipro and affecting some 40,000 people.

locations.name: Odesa
locations.summary: Odesa is Ukraine's main port and the outlet for its grain exports, which makes its harbour infrastructure a standing target. Russian forces never reached the city, and the naval threat receded after Ukraine pushed the Black Sea Fleet out of the western Black Sea. Strikes now fall on port facilities and the power grid; an attack on 9 August 2026 left the city in darkness.

keyEvents.text: Street clashes between rival demonstrators ended in a fire at the Trade Unions House; 42 died in the building and six in the earlier fighting.
keyEvents.note: DECIDE — see note below

keyEvents.text: The Black Sea Grain Initiative was signed in Istanbul, reopening the port to grain exports.
Russia withdrew from the grain deal and strikes on port infrastructure followed.
Missile strikes damaged the Transfiguration Cathedral, destroying its central altar.

locations.name: Sumy
locations.summary: Sumy sits on the Russian border in Ukraine's north-east and was partly overrun in the opening weeks of the invasion before Russian forces withdrew in April 2022. It served as the staging ground for Ukraine's incursion into Kursk oblast in August 2024, and drew a Russian counter-push into the northern part of the oblast after that operation ended. The city is within artillery and drone range and is struck routinely.

keyEvents.text: Russian columns crossed the border and parts of the oblast were occupied within days.
The governor declared the oblast clear of Russian troops.
keyEvents.note: CONTESTED: he said no settlements remained occupied on 4 April; 8 April is the declared completion

keyEvents.text: Ukraine launched its incursion into Kursk oblast from Sumy.
Two ballistic missiles struck the city centre on Palm Sunday, killing 35.

locations.name: Dnipro
locations.summary: Dnipro is the logistics and medical hub behind the eastern front, the city through which wounded soldiers and supplies move. It has never been threatened on the ground but is struck from the air; a missile hit an apartment block on 14 January 2023, killing forty-six people. Russian forces crossed into the surrounding oblast in 2025 and were pushed back out in a Ukrainian counteroffensive completed in August 2026.

keyEvents.text: A Kh-22 missile destroyed part of a nine-storey apartment block, killing 46 including six children.
Russia used the Oreshnik intermediate-range missile in combat for the first time, against the Pivdenmash plant.
A Ukrainian counteroffensive completed the recovery of occupied ground in Dnipropetrovsk oblast.

locations.name: Belgorod
locations.summary: Belgorod is the Russian city closest to the border, forty kilometres from Ukraine, and was a staging area for the invasion in 2022. It has been under Ukrainian shelling and drone attack since, which makes it the Russian city most exposed to the war. A drone attack on 9 August 2026 killed five people.

keyEvents.text: Two helicopters struck a fuel depot in the city in the first widely reported air strike on Russian soil; Ukraine did not claim responsibility and attribution remains disputed.
Fighters of the Russian Volunteer Corps and the Freedom of Russia Legion crossed into the oblast at Hraivoron.
Shelling of the city centre killed 25 including five children, the deadliest attack on a Russian city of the war.

locations.name: Kursk
locations.summary: Kursk oblast was the target of Ukraine's only sustained offensive onto Russian soil, launched on 6 August 2024, which seized the town of Sudzha and around a thousand square kilometres of territory. The ground proved impossible to hold. Russian forces, reinforced by North Korean troops, retook Sudzha in March 2025 and the campaign ended after 218 days.

keyEvents.text: Ukrainian forces crossed the border in the first sustained incursion by a foreign army into Russia since the Second World War.
Zelensky confirmed the capture of Sudzha.
keyEvents.note: CONTESTED: some accounts date effective control to 8–12 August

keyEvents.text: NATO and the Pentagon confirmed the deployment of North Korean troops to Kursk oblast.
Ukrainian forces withdrew from Sudzha and the campaign ended after 218 days.
keyEvents.note: CONTESTED: ISW and DeepState geolocated the withdrawal to 12 March; 16 March is Ukraine's General Staff confirmation

locations.name: Moscow
locations.summary: Moscow lies some 450 kilometres from Ukraine and was first reached by Ukrainian drones in 2023. The attacks have grown in scale since: Ukraine launched around six hundred drones towards the city in a single night in July 2026, and strikes have set the Moscow refinery alight more than once. They cause limited physical damage but repeatedly close the capital's airports.

keyEvents.text: Two drones were destroyed over the Kremlin.
Drones struck residential districts, the first attack on the capital's housing.
Around six hundred drones were launched towards the city in a single night.

locations.name: Novorossiysk
locations.summary: Novorossiysk is Russia's largest Black Sea port and became the main base for the Black Sea Fleet after Ukrainian strikes made Sevastopol untenable. It handles a large share of Russian oil and grain exports, which makes it a target of strategic rather than tactical value. A Ukrainian strike on the night of 11 August 2026 hit the naval base, oil terminals and grain facilities, and suspended operations at two major grain terminals.

keyEvents.text: Naval drones holed the landing ship Olenegorsky Gornyak in the harbour.
The Black Sea Fleet dispersed vessels from Sevastopol and Novorossiysk became its main working port.
keyEvents.note: note: a dispersal under fire, not a formal change of base

keyEvents.text: A large strike hit the naval base, oil terminals and grain facilities, suspending operations at two grain terminals.

locations.name: Nord Stream
locations.summary: Nord Stream 1 and 2 carried Russian gas under the Baltic Sea to Germany until underwater explosions ruptured both pipelines near the Danish island of Bornholm on 26 September 2022. No state has admitted responsibility. German prosecutors charged a former Ukrainian officer in July 2026 and allege the operation was ordered from Ukraine, which denies involvement; the pipelines have never returned to service.

keyEvents.text: Underwater explosions ruptured both Nord Stream pipelines near the Danish island of Bornholm, ending Russian pipeline gas to Germany.
Reporting revealed that Dutch intelligence had warned the CIA in June 2022 of a Ukrainian plan to attack the pipelines, and that the CIA had told Ukraine not to proceed.
German prosecutors issued an arrest warrant for a Ukrainian diver over the sabotage.
German prosecutors charged a former Ukrainian officer with directing an attack against civilian objects, alleging the operation was ordered from Ukraine.
Zelensky said Ukraine was not behind the sabotage and offered to assist the investigation.

name: Sudan civil war
summary: Fighting broke out on 15 April 2023 between Sudan's army and the Rapid Support Forces, a paramilitary group that had grown out of the Darfur militias, after a power struggle between their two commanders over the country's political transition turned into open war. The army holds the centre and east, including the recaptured capital; the RSF holds most of Darfur and runs a rival administration from Nyala. The war has produced the largest displacement crisis in the world and confirmed famine, and no peace process is under way. ---

locations.name: Khartoum
locations.summary: Khartoum is where the war began: on 15 April 2023 fighting erupted across the capital and the Rapid Support Forces held most of it within days, including the airport and much of the city centre. The army fought its way back over the following two years, retaking the Republican Palace on 21 March 2025 and clearing the last RSF positions from Khartoum state that May. The government returned from Port Sudan on 11 January 2026 to a capital largely destroyed.

keyEvents.text: Fighting erupted across the capital between the army and the Rapid Support Forces, and the RSF took most of the city within days.
The army retook the Republican Palace, the seat of government, after nearly two years of RSF control.
The army retook Khartoum International Airport and Burhan declared the capital free.
keyEvents.note: CONTESTED: some outlets date the declaration to 27 March

keyEvents.text: The government returned to Khartoum from Port Sudan after more than two years of war.

locations.name: Omdurman
locations.summary: Omdurman sits across the Nile from Khartoum and was divided between the two forces for most of the war. The army recaptured the national radio and television complex there on 12 March 2024, its first significant gain in the capital region, but fighting continued in the southern districts for another year. Salha, the last RSF stronghold, fell on 20 May 2025, and Khartoum state was declared clear of the RSF the same day.

keyEvents.text: The army recaptured the national radio and television complex, its first significant gain in the capital region.
The army took Salha, the last RSF stronghold in southern Omdurman, and declared Khartoum state entirely clear.

locations.name: El Fasher
locations.summary: El Fasher was the last city in Darfur still held by the army, and the RSF besieged it from May 2024. The siege lasted eighteen months, starved the displacement camps around the city and ended when the RSF stormed the army's divisional headquarters on 26 October 2025. Satellite imagery and UN investigators documented mass killings in the days that followed, and a UN fact-finding mission concluded in February 2026 that the events bore the hallmarks of genocide against the Fur and Zaghawa.

keyEvents.text: The RSF began its assault on the city, opening a siege that would last eighteen months.
keyEvents.note: CONTESTED: the UN dates the siege to "May 2024" without a day; Crisis Group dates the collapse of the local truce to 10-14 April 2024

keyEvents.text: The IPC confirmed famine in Zamzam camp outside the city, only the third famine determination in its history.
The RSF overran Zamzam camp, which held around 400,000 displaced people; a UN report later documented at least 1,013 civilians killed and 319 summarily executed.
The RSF stormed the army's divisional headquarters and took the city, ending the siege.
keyEvents.note: CONTESTED toll: the UN documented ~6,000 killed in the first three days; Yale researchers estimate ~60,000 over three weeks; the governor of Darfur said ~27,000. Do not cite a single figure.

keyEvents.text: A UN fact-finding mission concluded that the events at El Fasher bore the hallmarks of genocide against the Fur and Zaghawa.
keyEvents.note: CONTESTED: February 2026, exact day not established

locations.name: Nyala
locations.summary: Nyala is the largest city in Darfur and fell to the RSF on 26 October 2023, handing them the region's main airport and its principal supply hub. It has since become the seat of the parallel government that the RSF and its allies established, with Hemedti sworn in as chairman of its presidential council there on 30 August 2025. That administration holds no international recognition and represents the clearest step yet towards Sudan's partition.

keyEvents.text: The RSF stormed the army's last holdout in the city and took Nyala, the largest city in Darfur, with its airport and supply hub.
Hemedti was sworn in at Nyala as chairman of the presidential council of a parallel government, which holds no international recognition.
keyEvents.note: CONTESTED: the RSF announced the government on 15 April 2025 and named Nyala its seat in late July; 30 August is the swearing-in

locations.name: Port Sudan
locations.summary: Port Sudan on the Red Sea became the wartime capital after the government fled Khartoum in 2023, and it handles most of the aid entering the country. It went untouched until 4 May 2025, when RSF drones struck the airbase, the fuel depots and the power station over several consecutive days, ending the assumption that the east lay beyond the war's reach. The government returned to Khartoum in January 2026, but the port remains the country's lifeline.

keyEvents.text: RSF drones struck Port Sudan for the first time, hitting the Osman Digna airbase and, over the following days, fuel depots, the power station and the naval base.
keyEvents.note: CONTESTED: Wikipedia dates the first wave to 3 May; AFP, AP, Reuters and the Centre for Information Resilience all use 4 May

name: Gaza
summary: The war began on 7 October 2023, when Hamas-led fighters attacked southern Israel, killing around 1,200 people and taking about 250 hostage. Israel's campaign in response had killed more than 67,000 Palestinians by the time a ceasefire took effect on 10 October 2025, according to Gaza's health ministry. The ceasefire ended the full-scale war but not the dying, and Israel did not withdraw to its pre-war positions: it holds the majority of the Strip behind a demarcation called the Yellow Line. ---

locations.name: Gaza City
locations.summary: Gaza City was the main objective of Israel's ground invasion, which began on 27 October 2023 and encircled the city within weeks. Israeli forces raided al-Shifa, the territory's largest hospital, on 15 November 2023 and again on 18 March 2024, leaving it around 95 per cent destroyed by the WHO's assessment. The city sits on the Palestinian side of the Yellow Line, though eastern districts including al-Shujaiya were brought inside the Israeli-controlled zone in March 2026.

keyEvents.text: Israel launched its ground invasion of Gaza, and forces encircled the city within weeks.
Israeli forces raided al-Shifa Hospital, the territory's largest, having encircled it four days earlier; they withdrew on 24 November.
Israeli forces raided al-Shifa a second time in an operation lasting two weeks, after which the WHO assessed the hospital as around 95 per cent destroyed.
keyEvents.note: CONTESTED: the military said it killed 200+ militants and detained 500+; Gaza's health ministry said 200 displaced people were killed inside

keyEvents.text: Israel extended its restricted zone beyond the Yellow Line, bringing al-Shujaiya in eastern Gaza City inside it and cutting aid access.
keyEvents.note: CONTESTED: reported by NPR and Reuters as a separate "orange zone"; Al Jazeera describes the same change as the Yellow Line itself moving. Mid-March; exact day not established

locations.name: Khan Younis
locations.summary: Khan Younis became the focus of the campaign once Gaza City had fallen, with Israeli operations opening on 1 December 2023 and a formal siege running from late January 2024. Israeli forces withdrew on 7 April 2024 but returned repeatedly over the following months, so the withdrawal marked a phase rather than an ending. Much of the city now lies behind the Yellow Line, and it is where Palestinians returning through Rafah are taken.

keyEvents.text: Israel opened its operation against Khan Younis, expanding ground forces into southern Gaza two days later.
Israeli forces withdrew from Khan Younis in a broader southern pullback, though they re-entered repeatedly later that year.

locations.name: Rafah
locations.summary: Rafah sits on the Egyptian border and became the last refuge of the war, sheltering more than 1.4 million displaced people by early 2024 and briefly becoming the most populous city in the Palestinian territories. Israel launched its offensive there on 6 May 2024 and took the border crossing the next day, closing the only route out of Gaza that Israel does not otherwise control. The crossing reopened on 2 February 2026, on foot, for roughly fifty people a day.

keyEvents.text: Israel launched its offensive on Rafah, where more than 1.4 million displaced people had been sheltering.
Israeli forces took the Rafah border crossing, closing Gaza's only exit not otherwise under Israeli control.
The Rafah crossing reopened for the first time since May 2024, on foot and limited to around fifty people a day, with more than 13,000 patients still awaiting medical evacuation.

locations.name: Jabalia
locations.summary: Jabalia is the largest of Gaza's refugee camps, built for those displaced in 1948, and among the most densely populated places anywhere. Israeli airstrikes hit it on 31 October and 1 November 2023; Amnesty International found no evidence of a military objective in the first and called it a likely war crime. The camp has been fought over repeatedly since and lies close to the Yellow Line.

keyEvents.text: An Israeli airstrike hit the al-Trans area of the camp.
keyEvents.note: CONTESTED toll: a UN investigation verified at least 42 killed including 14 children; local figures ran far higher. Amnesty International found no evidence of a military objective and called it a likely war crime

keyEvents.text: A second airstrike hit the camp, killing at least 80 according to Gaza's civil defence.
An airstrike hit the al-Fakhoura school, run by UNRWA and sheltering displaced people, killing 15.
